subject: Automotive & EVs
title: Liability: Who Is at Fault?
description: One-minute skill: Liability: Who Is at Fault?.

hook.text: When a human driver crashes, they're at fault. When a robot crashes, the question gets complicated.

buildup.text: Is the carmaker liable? The software company? The sensor supplier? The passenger who wasn't watching?

discovery.text: Mercedes became the first to accept legal liability for crashes in Level 3 mode—a historic move.

twist.text: Most other companies use fine print to keep liability with the driver, even during automated driving.

climax.text: Until liability laws catch up with the technology, every autonomous crash will spark a legal battle.

punchline.text: The law hasn't decided who's driving a self-driving car.

quiz.question: Which automaker first accepted legal liability for Level 3 crashes?

details.summary: When a self-driving car crashes, determining legal liability is complex, potentially falling on the manufacturer, software developer, sensor supplier, or even the human who chose to use autonomous mode.
details.whyItMatters: Liability frameworks will determine whether manufacturers are willing to deploy autonomous vehicles and whether insurance models can adapt. Unclear liability is a major barrier to AV adoption.
takeaways: Traditional liability assumes a human driver is responsible
Autonomous vehicles shift potential blame to the manufacturer
No country has fully resolved AV liability law yet

faq.question: Who pays when an autonomous car causes an accident?
faq.answer: It depends on the autonomy level. At Level 2, the driver is liable. At Level 4 and above, liability shifts toward the manufacturer. Mercedes has accepted liability for crashes when its Level 3 system is engaged.

faq.question: How will insurance work for self-driving cars?
faq.answer: Insurance may shift from individual driver policies to manufacturer product liability coverage. Some predict insurance costs will decrease overall because autonomous vehicles should eventually have fewer accidents than human drivers.
